column1: 1:1|The Song of Songs, which belongs to Solomon.|Retain superlative title and open Solomonic relation.
1:2|Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth!\nYour caresses are better than wine.|Retain sudden third-to-second-person shift and bodily desire.
1:3|Your oils give off a lovely fragrance;\nyour name is oil poured out.\nThat is why the young women love you.|Keep name/oil image and young women’s attraction.

1:4|Draw me after you—let us run!
The king has brought me into his rooms.
We will rejoice and delight in you;
we will celebrate your caresses more than wine.
Rightly do they love you.|Preserve singular/plural shifts without imposing one speaker scheme.

1:5|I am black and beautiful,
daughters of Jerusalem,
like the tents of Kedar,
like Solomon’s curtains.|Render conjunction affirmatively and retain named comparisons.

1:6|Do not stare at me because I am dark,
because the sun has gazed on me.
My mother’s sons were angry with me;
they made me guard the vineyards.
My own vineyard I did not guard.|Keep sun’s gaze, brothers’ coercion, and vineyard ambiguity.

1:7|Tell me, you whom my whole being loves,
where you graze your flock,
where you make it rest at noon.
Why should I be like a veiled woman
beside your companions’ flocks?|Preserve shepherd setting and veiled reading with note.

1:8|If you do not know, most beautiful of women,
follow the tracks of the flock
and graze your young goats
beside the shepherds’ tents.|Keep reply to female addressee and practical pastoral images.
1:9|My love, I compare you to my mare\namong Pharaoh’s chariots.|Retain surprising female horse and Pharaoh image.
1:10|Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments,\nyour neck with strings of beads.|Keep adornment of cheeks and neck.
1:11|We will make you ornaments of gold\nstudded with silver.|Preserve plural makers and two metals.
1:12|While the king was reclining at his table,\nmy nard released its fragrance.|Keep first-person fragrance and banquet setting.
1:13|My beloved is a pouch of myrrh to me,\nresting between my breasts.|Preserve intimate bodily perfume image.
1:14|My beloved is a cluster of henna blossoms to me\nin the vineyards of En-gedi.|Keep plant and specific place.
1:15|How beautiful you are, my love!\nHow beautiful!\nYour eyes are doves.|Preserve repeated praise and direct dove metaphor.
1:16|How handsome you are, my beloved,\nhow delightful!\nOur bed is green and flourishing.|Reflect masculine address and living bed image.
1:17|The beams of our houses are cedars;\nour rafters are cypresses.|Retain architectural tree imagery and read-form rafters.
2:1|I am a meadow flower of Sharon,\na lily of the valleys.|Avoid unsupported certainty of rose species; retain self-description.
2:2|Like a lily among thorns,\nso is my love among the young women.|Keep lover’s response and thorn contrast.

2:3|Like an apple tree among forest trees,
so is my beloved among the young men.
I delight to sit in his shade;
his fruit is sweet to my palate.|Preserve sensory tree metaphor and male comparison.
2:4|He brought me into the house of wine;\nhis banner over me was love.|Keep wine house and banner image with alternative noted.
2:5|Sustain me with raisin cakes;\nrefresh me with apples,\nfor I am sick with love.|Retain foods and lovesickness as bodily metaphor.
2:6|His left hand is beneath my head,\nand his right arm embraces me.|Preserve left/right and actual embrace.

2:7|I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles or the does of the field:
do not stir up or awaken love
until it wishes.|Keep animal oath, paired verbs, and love’s own timing.

2:8|The sound of my beloved!
Look, he is coming,
leaping over mountains,
bounding over hills.|Retain exclamation and parallel motion.

2:9|My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag.
Look, he stands behind our wall,
looking through the windows,
peering through the lattice.|Keep animal comparison and three spatial details.
2:10|My beloved speaks to me:\n“Rise, my love, my beautiful one,\nand come away.|Make quotation boundary audible without extra characterization.
2:11|Look, winter has passed;\nthe rain is over and gone.|Retain doubled departure of rainy season.
2:12|Flowers appear on the earth;\nthe season of singing has arrived,\nand the turtledove’s voice is heard in our land.|Choose singing with pruning alternative in note.

2:13|The fig tree is ripening its early fruit;
blossoming vines give off their fragrance.
Rise, my love, my beautiful one,
and come away.|Preserve seasonal produce and repeated invitation.

2:14|My dove in the rock’s clefts,
in the hiding place of the steep cliffs,
let me see your face,
let me hear your voice.
Your voice is sweet,
and your face is lovely.”|Retain concealed dove and paired requests.
2:15|Catch us the foxes,\nthe little foxes ruining the vineyards,\nfor our vineyards are in bloom.|Keep plural command and vineyard vulnerability without decoding symbolism.
2:16|My beloved is mine, and I am his;\nhe grazes among the lilies.|Retain mutual belonging and grazing image.

2:17|Until the day breathes and the shadows flee,
turn, my beloved.
Be like a gazelle or a young stag
on the cleft mountains.|Keep day’s breath and uncertain Bether interpretation in note.
3:1|On my bed, night after night,\nI sought the one my whole being loves.\nI sought him but did not find him.|Retain repeated seeking and plural nights.

3:2|“I will get up and go through the city,
through its streets and squares,
to seek the one my whole being loves.”
I sought him but did not find him.|Keep resolve, civic spaces, and exact search refrain.
3:3|The watchmen found me\nas they made their rounds in the city.\n“Have you seen the one my whole being loves?”|Preserve reversal from seeking to being found.

3:4|Scarcely had I passed them
when I found the one my whole being loves.
I held him and would not let him go
until I brought him to my mother’s house,
to the room of the woman who conceived me.|Retain active woman and maternal room specificity.

3:5|I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles or the does of the field:
do not stir up or awaken love
until it wishes.|Match repeated oath exactly.

3:6|Who is this coming up from the wilderness
like columns of smoke,
fragrant with myrrh and frankincense,
with all the merchant’s scented powders?|Keep question and procession’s scented imagery.
3:7|Look! Solomon’s litter!\nSixty warriors surround it,\nwarriors of Israel.|Retain sixty and Israel repetition.

3:8|All of them grip the sword,
trained for battle,
each with his sword at his thigh
against the terrors of the night.|Preserve martial protection and night fears.
3:9|King Solomon made himself a carriage\nfrom the wood of Lebanon.|Keep named king, carriage, and wood source.

3:10|He made its posts of silver,
its support of gold,
its seat of purple cloth,
its interior inlaid with love
from the daughters of Jerusalem.|Preserve unusual love-inlay wording with uncertainty noted.

3:11|Come out, daughters of Zion,
and look at King Solomon
wearing the crown his mother gave him
on his wedding day,
the day his heart rejoiced.|Retain Zion address, mother, and doubled day.

4:1|How beautiful you are, my love!
How beautiful!
Your eyes are doves behind your veil.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
streaming down Mount Gilead.|Keep refrain, veil, and moving goat image.

4:2|Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep
coming up from washing,
each bearing twins,
none bereaved among them.|Retain twin/bereaved imagery rather than explain matching teeth.

4:3|Your lips are a scarlet thread;
your mouth is lovely.
Your temples are slices of pomegranate
behind your veil.|Keep thread, color, fruit, and veil.

4:4|Your neck is like David’s tower,
built in courses;
a thousand shields hang on it,
all the shields of warriors.|Keep thousand and uncertain construction term in note.
4:5|Your two breasts are like two fawns,\ntwins of a gazelle,\ngrazing among the lilies.|Retain breasts and doubled two image without euphemism.
4:6|Until the day breathes and the shadows flee,\nI will go to the mountain of myrrh\nand the hill of frankincense.|Match day phrase and preserve aromatic landscape.
4:7|You are beautiful in every part, my love;\nthere is no blemish in you.|Retain whole-person praise without theological import.

4:9|You have captured my heart, my sister, my bride;
you have captured my heart
with one glance of your eyes,
with one jewel of your necklace.|Preserve doubled heart capture and sister/bride endearment.
4:10|How lovely your caresses, my sister, my bride!\nHow much better than wine!\nThe fragrance of your oils surpasses every spice.|Keep repeated kin/endearment and sensory comparisons.
4:11|Your lips drip nectar, bride;\nhoney and milk are beneath your tongue.\nYour clothes smell like Lebanon.|Retain tactile and geographic scents.
4:12|A locked garden is my sister, my bride,\na locked spring, a sealed fountain.|Preserve enclosed garden and two water sources; note gal uncertainty.
4:13|Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates\nwith choice fruits,\nhenna with nard,|Keep garden catalogue beginning across verse boundary.

4:14|nard and saffron, sweet cane and cinnamon,
with every frankincense tree,
myrrh and aloes,
with all the finest spices.|Retain repeated nard and full aromatic list.
4:15|You are a garden fountain,\na well of living water,\nstreams flowing from Lebanon.|Preserve living water and mountain source.

4:16|Wake, north wind! Come, south wind!
Blow through my garden; let its spices flow.
Let my beloved come into his garden
and eat its choice fruits.|Retain woman’s invitation and my/his garden shift.

5:1|I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.
I have gathered my myrrh with my spice,
eaten my honeycomb with my honey,
drunk my wine with my milk.
Eat, friends! Drink deeply, lovers!|Keep completed first-person actions and plural invitation without assigning new speaker dogmatically.

5:2|I was asleep, but my heart was awake.
The sound of my beloved knocking!
“Open to me, my sister, my love,
my dove, my perfect one.
My head is drenched with dew,
my hair with the drops of night.”|Retain waking/dream tension and four endearments.

5:3|“I have taken off my tunic—
how can I put it on again?
I have washed my feet—
how can I dirty them?”|Preserve doubled reluctance questions.
5:4|My beloved reached his hand through the opening,\nand my inward parts stirred for him.|Keep opening and bodily arousal without overexplaining.

5:5|I rose to open to my beloved.
My hands dripped myrrh,
my fingers flowing myrrh
on the handles of the bolt.|Preserve perfume and door mechanism.

5:6|I opened to my beloved,
but my beloved had slipped away, gone.
My very life went out when he spoke.
I sought him but did not find him;
I called, but he did not answer.|Retain difficult when-he-spoke chronology and failed search.

5:7|The watchmen found me
as they made their rounds in the city.
They struck me; they wounded me.
The guards of the walls
took my wrap from me.|Keep assault explicit and distinguish no imagined rescue.
5:8|I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem:\nif you find my beloved, what will you tell him?\nThat I am sick with love.|Retain question-and-answer oath form.

5:9|How is your beloved more than another beloved,
most beautiful of women?
How is your beloved more than another beloved,
that you put us under such an oath?|Preserve repeated challenge and female address.
5:10|My beloved is radiant and ruddy,\nstanding out among ten thousand.|Keep complexion imagery and exact number.
5:11|His head is finest gold;\nhis hair falls in curls,\nblack as a raven.|Retain mixed precious-metal and living color images.

5:12|His eyes are like doves beside streams of water,\nbathed in milk,\nsecurely set.|Make the obscure fullness-setting phrase readable as securely fitted eyes; retain dove and milk images and note uncertainty.

5:13|His cheeks are beds of spice,
mounds of fragrant herbs.
His lips are lilies
dripping flowing myrrh.|Retain garden, lips, and liquid perfume.

5:14|His arms are rods of gold
set with beryl.
His abdomen is polished ivory
overlaid with sapphires.|Preserve bodily jewel imagery, note ancient stone uncertainty.

5:15|His legs are pillars of marble
set on bases of fine gold.
His appearance is like Lebanon,
choice as its cedars.|Keep architecture and landscape as parallel praise.

5:16|His mouth is sweetness itself;
every part of him is desirable.
This is my beloved, this is my friend,
daughters of Jerusalem.|Preserve desire and friend alongside beloved.

6:1|Where has your beloved gone,
most beautiful of women?
Which way did your beloved turn?
We will seek him with you.|Keep plural offer and repeated beloved.

6:2|My beloved has gone down to his garden,
to the beds of spice,
to graze in the gardens
and gather lilies.|Retain pastoral/garden ambiguity.
6:3|I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine;\nhe grazes among the lilies.|Preserve reversed order from2:16 and repeated grazing.
6:4|You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love,\nlovely as Jerusalem,\nawesome as troops with banners.|Keep two cities and military comparison.

6:5|Turn your eyes away from me;
they overwhelm me.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
streaming down from Gilead.|Retain power of gaze and repeated goat image with source distinction.

6:6|Your teeth are like a flock of ewes
coming up from washing,
each bearing twins,
none bereaved among them.|Preserve repeated twin metaphor but ewes rather than shorn sheep.
6:7|Your temples are slices of pomegranate\nbehind your veil.|Match repeated praise from4:3.
6:8|There may be sixty queens,\neighty concubines,\nand young women beyond counting,|Retain exact harem categories and numbers.

6:9|but my dove, my perfect one, is unique,
her mother’s only one,
the cherished one of her who bore her.
Young women saw her and called her fortunate;
queens and concubines praised her.|Keep unique/only language and women’s praise.

6:10|“Who is this looking out like the dawn,
beautiful as the moon,
clear as the sun,
awesome as troops with banners?”|Retain luminous progression and banner refrain.

6:11|I went down to the nut orchard
to see the valley’s new growth,
to see whether the vines had budded
and the pomegranates were in bloom.|Keep unspecified first-person speaker and botanical inspection.
6:12|Before I knew it, my desire had set me\namong the chariots of my noble people.|Retain difficult soul/chariots phrase with alternatives in note.

6:13|Return, return, Shulammite!
Return, return, so we may look at you!
Why would you look at the Shulammite
as at a dance of two camps?|Map source7:1 to public6:13; retain four returns and question.
7:1|How lovely your steps in sandals, noble daughter!\nThe curves of your thighs are like jewels,\nthe work of a craftsman’s hands.|Map source7:2 to public7:1; retain thighs and skilled craft.

7:2|Your navel is a rounded bowl—
may it never lack mixed wine.
Your belly is a heap of wheat
ringed with lilies.|Retain bodily and agricultural images without euphemism.
7:3|Your two breasts are like two fawns,\ntwins of a gazelle.|Preserve shortened recurring simile.

7:4|Your neck is an ivory tower.
Your eyes are pools in Heshbon,
by the gate of Bath-rabbim.
Your nose is like Lebanon’s tower
looking toward Damascus.|Retain all body parts, places, and viewing direction.
7:5|Your head crowns you like Carmel;\nyour flowing hair is like purple cloth.\nA king is held captive in its tresses.|Keep royal captivity by hair image.
7:6|How beautiful, how delightful you are,\nlove with all your pleasures!|Retain address as love and sensuous plural pleasures.
7:7|Your stature is like a palm tree,\nyour breasts like its clusters.|Keep body/tree correspondence.

7:8|I said, “I will climb the palm
and take hold of its branches.”
May your breasts be like clusters of grapes,
your breath fragrant as apples,|Retain first-person resolve and ensuing wishes.
7:9|and your mouth like fine wine—\ngoing down smoothly for my beloved,\nstirring the lips of sleepers.|Preserve sudden my-beloved shift, pinned sleepers reading, and wine stirring their lips.
7:10|I am my beloved’s,\nand his desire is for me.|Keep woman’s declaration and desire directed toward her.
7:11|Come, my beloved, let us go out to the fields;\nlet us spend the night in the villages.|Retain woman’s initiative and rural lodging.

7:12|Let us rise early for the vineyards
to see whether the vines have budded,
whether the blossoms have opened
and the pomegranates are in bloom.
There I will give you my caresses.|Keep shared inspection and explicit woman’s gift of affection.

7:13|The mandrakes give off their scent,
and at our doors are all kinds of choice fruits,
new and old,
which I have stored for you, my beloved.|Retain mandrakes, two ages of fruit, and stored gift.

8:1|If only you were like a brother to me,
nursed at my mother’s breasts!
Then, finding you outside, I could kiss you,
and no one would despise me.|Preserve counterfactual brother comparison and public affection’s constraint.

8:2|I would lead you and bring you to my mother’s house,
where she would teach me.
I would give you spiced wine to drink,
the juice of my pomegranate.|Choose mother as teacher with alternative you in note.
8:3|His left hand is beneath my head,\nand his right arm embraces me.|Match embrace refrain.
8:4|I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem:\nwhy stir up or awaken love\nbefore it wishes?|Retain changed interrogative oath without adding absent animals.

8:5|Who is this coming up from the wilderness,
leaning on her beloved?
Under the apple tree I awakened you;
there your mother labored with you,
there she who bore you was in labor.|Preserve gender transition and doubled birth memory.

8:6|Set me like a seal on your heart,
like a seal on your arm.
For love is strong as death,
jealousy relentless as Sheol.
Its flashes are flashes of fire,
a flame of **YAH**.|Retain jealousy, Sheol, and divided divine-name source with alternative noted.

8:7|Many waters cannot extinguish love;
rivers cannot sweep it away.
If a man offered all his household wealth for love,
he would be utterly scorned.|Keep resistance to flood and unpurchasable love.

8:8|We have a little sister,
and she has no breasts yet.
What shall we do for our sister
on the day she is spoken for?|Preserve family’s question about immature sister without assigning age.

8:9|If she is a wall,
we will build a silver turret on her.
If she is a door,
we will enclose her with a cedar plank.|Keep conditional family construction images without interpretive substitution.

8:10|I am a wall,
and my breasts are towers.
Then in his eyes I became
like one who finds peace.|Retain woman’s reply, bodily maturity, and peace word.
8:11|Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon.\nHe entrusted it to keepers;\neach was to bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit.|Preserve owner, place, entrusted cultivation, and amount.

8:12|My vineyard, my own, is in my keeping.\nThe thousand are yours, Solomon,\nand two hundred for those who keep its fruit.|Retain emphatic ownership and literal before-me relation without adding a decision to give the vineyard; preserve distinct amounts.
8:13|You who dwell in the gardens,\ncompanions are listening for your voice.\nLet me hear it!|Retain female addressee and singular request among listeners.
8:14|Hurry away, my beloved!\nBe like a gazelle or a young stag\non the mountains of spices.|Keep imperative escape and recurring gazelle imagery at open ending.
